speaker_role: current international admissions officer at Harvard College, interviewed by a Harvard sophomore student
commercial_incentive: None evident; official Harvard admissions office podcast/channel.
key_insights: Harvard has dedicated international admissions officers assigned to specific world regions who understand each region's grading systems, national exams, and course types.
International financial aid is 'need-blind and need-based' exactly like domestic aid: admission decisions don't factor in ability to pay, and demonstrated need is met afterward.
Students from countries without AP/honors systems are evaluated on whether they took the most rigorous curriculum available within their own school, not against a US-style framework.

Officer encourages applicants to reach out with questions before and during the process (including after being deferred, to send meaningful updates), saying this is expected and appreciated, not seen as a bother.

Officer describes the US liberal arts model (explore broadly before declaring, e.g., switching away from an intended computer science path) as something many international families don't initially understand, contrasted with direct-to-professional-school systems elsewhere.

First-year international students get a proctor (live-in adult), a peer advising fellow (PAF), an academic adviser, the Woodbridge International Society, and a student-led international preorientation program covering practical needs like opening a bank account.
International students can study abroad while at Harvard (financial aid travels with them), and have access to the Harvard International Office for visa and on-campus work questions.
notable_or_distinctive: Direct confirmation from a Harvard admissions officer that international aid is need-blind/need-based identically to domestic aid, plus detail on region-specific reader assignments and international-specific campus support structures (Woodbridge International Society, international preorientation).
reliability_notes: Official first-person source, so reliable for Harvard's own stated policy, but specific to Harvard and not necessarily representative of other schools' international admissions/aid practices.
